newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish motorways deny gov't pressure to cut tolls.
newsitem.headline: Spanish motorways deny gov't pressure to cut tolls.

text.p: Spain's association of motorway firms ASETA denied on Tuesday any pressure from the government to cut tolls, responding to financial press reports indicating that this was the case.
"ASETA wants to state that none of its associates has received pressure from the Development Ministry to reduce tariffs," a statement said.
Financial daily La Gaceta de los Negocios reported that the government was trying to force a cut in motorway tolls, reducing internal rates of return (IRR).
Spokesmen both at the Development Industry and ASETA confirmed that talks were under way, but ASETA said these were "about operating (motorway) concessions, and aimed at leaving IRRs unchanged."
At the end of 1996, the Spanish government said motorway tolls were to fall around eight percent from September 1, 1997.

That would meet one of the main points of the political agreement between the minority Popular Party government and Catalonia's Convergence and Unity which holds the balance of power in Spain. The northwestern region has the biggest concentration of toll motoways.

In December 1996 the government suggested, Brussels allowing, it could compensate motorway firms for the reduction in toll income reducing value-added tax to seven percent from the present 16 percent. If the European Union did not give the go-ahead, the government would study different solutions.
ASETA manages about 2,100 kms of motorways in Spain. The four biggest motorway firms are Acesa, Aumar, Europistas and Iberpistas.
